traveler: Carmen Miranda (Maria do Carmo Miranda da Cunha)
title: The Milliner's Turban: Portugal, Rio, Broadway, and the Fruit That Ate the Woman
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Várzea da Ovelha e Aliviada, the birth in the parish
stops.date_confidence: attested; the coordinate is contested, three different fixes circulate for this parish and Wikidata's is used here
stops.campa: In a parish of the Douro hills near Marco de Canaveses, Maria do Carmo Miranda da Cunha is born to a barber and amateur musician, José Maria Pinto da Cunha, and his wife Maria Emília Miranda. Portugal is still a monarchy; the countryside is emptying toward Brazil. Her father loves Bizet and calls the second daughter Carmen. No plaque marks the house. The parish itself is dissolved in the administrative reorganization of 2013 and folded into Várzea, Aliviada e Folhada, so the place of her birth no longer exists under the name the register gives it.
suggested_refs: The baptismal register of Várzea da Ovelha e Aliviada, Marco de Canaveses, February 1909
sources: Observador (2015), 'Carmen Miranda, a baiana que nasceu em Marco de Canaveses'

stops.name: Praça Mauá, the family comes ashore
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: José Maria has gone ahead to Rio de Janeiro; Maria Emília follows with Olinda and the infant Carmen, not yet one year old, and the family is reunited in the city that will keep her. They come ashore at the passenger docks of Praça Mauá, the mouth through which Brazil takes in European labor by the shipload. The exact pier is unrecorded. She will cross this water again in thirty years, in the other direction, as a manufactured export, and these same docks will receive her coffin in August 1955.
suggested_refs: The Praça Mauá passenger docks, Rio de Janeiro, principal immigrant landing of the period

stops.name: Travessa do Comércio, the house in the old town
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the street is named by secondary biographical accounts, the house number by none
stops.campa: The family settles on a narrow colonial lane behind Praça XV, in the old commercial center a few streets from the bay. Four more children are born here: Amaro in 1912, Cecília in 1913, Aurora in 1915, Óscar in 1916. Aurora will become a film star too and will act beside her sister. The lane survives, cobbled and low, into the present century. Biographers name it; no document in the reachable record fixes the house, and none names the street either.
suggested_refs: Travessa do Comércio, Rio de Janeiro, the surviving colonial lane named in the biographical literature
sources: Cinema Clássico, 'Carmen Miranda: Do Cassino da Urca a Hollywood'

stops.name: Convent of Saint Therese of Lisieux, the school
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the school is attested, the years are not given in the reachable sourcing
stops.campa: She is put to school with the nuns at the Convent of Saint Therese of Lisieux, named for the Carmelite dead in 1897 and canonized in 1925, when Carmen is sixteen and long out of the classroom. The education is conventional for the daughter of poor immigrants and it does not last; the household needs wages more than a schooled daughter. English Wikipedia names the convent. No reachable source fixes its address in Rio, so the stop sits on the city-center coordinate rather than on the building itself.
suggested_refs: The Convent of Saint Therese of Lisieux, Rio de Janeiro, location unconfirmed

stops.name: Downtown Rio, the necktie shop at fourteen
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the age is given as about fourteen, the year is derived from it
stops.campa: At about fourteen she takes work in a tie shop in the downtown streets to help pay for the treatment of her older sister Olinda, who has tuberculosis. It is the first wage of a working life that will not stop: counter, needle, hat block, microphone, soundstage. The shop is not named in any surviving account, and the coordinate is a general fix on the commercial district. Nothing about the girl behind the counter is recorded by anyone who saw her there; the record of her begins later, with the voice.
suggested_refs: The downtown Rio necktie trade of the early 1920s, her first documented employment

stops.name: Downtown Rio, the hat trade
stops.date_confidence: traditional; sources give the mid-1920s without a year
stops.campa: She moves to a boutique, learns to block and trim hats, and opens a millinery business of her own. The trade teaches her what she will spend her life doing: building an object that sits on a head and tells strangers, at a glance, what to think. Customers hear her singing over the work. The turbans that Hollywood will pile with wax fruit are built on this apprenticeship, and she goes on designing her own costumes long after a studio wardrobe department is paid to do it for her. The shop's name is not consistent across sources.
suggested_refs: Her Rio millinery business of the mid-1920s, name and address unrecorded

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the first record with Josué de Barros
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The composer Josué de Barros hears her sing at the family boarding house and takes her into a studio. 'Não Vá Simbora' is cut this year for Brunswick, not for RCA Victor, which several accounts give and which is wrong by a label and a year. The record does not make her. It makes her a singer, which is a different thing: the milliner now has two trades, and within twelve months only one of them will matter. De Barros walks her into the studio and then drops out of the story people tell about her.
suggested_refs: The Brunswick Records pressing of 'Não Vá Simbora,' Rio de Janeiro, 1929

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, RCA Victor and Taí
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: She records 'Pra Você Gostar de Mim,' known everywhere as 'Taí,' written by Joubert de Carvalho. It sells thirty-five thousand copies and RCA Victor signs her to two years. She is twenty-one and the leading interpreter of samba in a country that has just decided samba is its national music. The song stays fastened to her name for the rest of her life and past it. In 1932 she appears in the sound documentary O Carnaval Cantado no Rio, the first time anyone photographs her singing.
suggested_refs: The RCA Victor recording of 'Pra Você Gostar de Mim' (Taí), Joubert de Carvalho, 1930

stops.name: Rádio Mayrink Veiga, the first contracted singer
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the station address is approximate, placed in the Cinelândia district
stops.campa: Rádio Mayrink Veiga signs her as the first contracted singer in the history of Brazilian broadcasting, on a two-year term, and she becomes the highest-paid voice on the air. The announcer César Ladeira gives her the name the country will use: A Pequena Notável, the Little Notable One. Radio is reaching the interior for the first time and she reaches it with radio. The station coordinate is approximate; the sourcing gathered names the station and the contract, not the address.
suggested_refs: The Rádio Mayrink Veiga contract of 1933, first singer's contract in Brazilian broadcasting

stops.name: Rádio Tupi, the year across the dial
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted, station address approximate
stops.campa: For one year she moves across the dial to Rádio Tupi, still commanding the top fee in Brazilian broadcasting. She is making films as well now, carrying a persona built for the microphone into a medium that watches as well as listens. Two stations bid over one singer, which no Brazilian performer before her has been worth. When the year is up she goes back. The station coordinate is approximate; the sourcing gathered names the station and the year of the move, not the address.
suggested_refs: Rádio Tupi, Rio de Janeiro, her single-year engagement of 1937

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the Miranda sisters on film
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: She appears in Alô, Alô, Brasil! and becomes the most popular figure in Brazilian cinema; the same year Estudantes gives her a first speaking role. In 1936 Alô, Alô, Carnaval! puts her onscreen beside her sister Aurora, the two Miranda girls from Travessa do Comércio singing in a film about a radio show, which is what their lives already are. The Brazilian film industry of the decade is built largely out of carnival numbers strung on thin plots, and she is its reason for existing.
suggested_refs: Alô, Alô, Brasil! (1935) and Alô, Alô, Carnaval! (1936), Cinédia, Rio de Janeiro

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, Banana da Terra and the fruit turban
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: In Banana da Terra she comes onstage in the baiana: the dress of the Afro-Brazilian street vendors of Salvador, stylized, jeweled, topped with fruit. She sings 'O Que É Que A Baiana Tem?' and the costume becomes the image. The fruit is never real. No verified record places her performing in Bahia, whose women's dress she wears in nearly every film she will make; the costume travels where she does not. She builds it herself, out of the milliner's trade, before any studio has an opinion about it.
stops.quote: In Brazil in Bahia, the girls carry the basket with the fruits on her head, and they have big bracelets and big necklaces and they sell fruits in the streets and I take it from the girls.
stops.quote_source: Carmen Miranda, London interview, 1948, quoted in NPR, Of Fruit Hats And Happy Tropics, A Renaissance For Carmen Miranda (2015)
suggested_refs: Banana da Terra (1939) and the baiana costume of Bahian street vendors

stops.name: Cassino da Urca, Lee Shubert in the audience
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted, and the casino is demolished so the coordinate is the historic site
stops.campa: Lee Shubert, in Rio looking for an act, watches her at the Cassino da Urca, a gambling house and revue theater under Sugarloaf where Rio's money and Rio's foreigners meet. He offers eight weeks on Broadway. She accepts on condition that her band comes with her: the Bando da Lua, six Brazilian musicians, because she will not be accompanied by Americans playing at samba. The Brazilian government pays their passage, having decided that what she carries north is national property.
suggested_refs: The Cassino da Urca, Rio de Janeiro, demolished; summit of the city's nightlife in the 1930s
sources: Cinema Clássico, 'Carmen Miranda: Do Cassino da Urca a Hollywood'

stops.name: Port of Rio de Janeiro, the SS Uruguay sails
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: She sails from the Rio docks aboard the SS Uruguay with the Bando da Lua and the costumes, sent off by a country that expects her to carry its music into a nation that has never heard it. Getúlio Vargas's Estado Novo is manufacturing a Brazilian national identity and has decided she is one of its exports. Five months earlier, across the same city, Arthur Bispo do Rosário was committed to the Colônia Juliano Moreira: one Rio, one government, one citizen locked away and one sent abroad as the country's face.
suggested_refs: The SS Uruguay, Moore-McCormack Lines, sailing of 4 May 1939

stops.name: Manhattan pier, the arrival
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pier is not named in the sourcing, the coordinate is the Hudson River passenger district of the period
stops.campa: The Uruguay docks in New York after two weeks at sea. She has almost no English and a repertoire in a language nobody on the pier speaks. The press meets the boat because Shubert has arranged for the press to meet the boat. Within four years she will be the highest-paid entertainer in the United States. The first thing she is quoted saying in an American newspaper is a joke about the size of her English vocabulary, and the joke is repeated for the rest of her life and after it.
stops.quote: I say money, money, money and I say hot dog! I say yes, no, and I say money, money, money.
stops.quote_source: Carmen Miranda, first American press interview, New York World-Telegram, 1939, quoted in Encyclopedia of World Biography via Encyclopedia.com
suggested_refs: The Hudson River passenger piers of Manhattan, arrival of 18 May 1939

stops.name: Broadhurst Theatre, The Streets of Paris
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: She opens at the Broadhurst in the revue The Streets of Paris, speaks four words of English onstage, sings in Portuguese to an audience that understands none of it, and stops the show. The reviews are excellent and the New York papers give her a name within days: the Brazilian Bombshell. The World's Fair is drawing the crowds out to Queens, and the press decides she is the girl who saved Broadway from it. Eight weeks are contracted. She will not live in Brazil again.
stops.quote: South American contributes the [revue's] most magnetic personality.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Brooks Atkinson, New York Times review of The Streets of Paris, June 1939, as quoted in English Wikipedia; the bracketed word is an editorial insertion and the original Times text could not be reached [R]
suggested_refs: The Streets of Paris, Broadhurst Theatre, opened 19 June 1939

stops.name: The White House, presented to Roosevelt
stops.date_confidence: the presentation is attested; the date is not consistently given and the sourcing spreads it across 1939 to 1941, so the year is defaulted
stops.campa: She is presented to Franklin Roosevelt and performs with the Bando da Lua, folded into the Good Neighbor Policy: hemispheric goodwill assembled out of entertainment and run through Nelson Rockefeller's Office of Inter-American Affairs. The same office sends George Balanchine's American Ballet Caravan to Buenos Aires and Rio in 1941, and the same Rockefeller had Diego Rivera's mural chiseled off a Rockefeller Center wall. Washington wants an exportable Latin America. She is polled the third most popular personality in the country.
suggested_refs: The Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs and its cultural-diplomacy program, 1940-1945
sources: themovierat.com, 'Carmen Miranda, The Three Caballeros and the Good Neighbor Policy'

stops.name: New York, Down Argentine Way shot away from Hollywood
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted, and the specific stage is not identified
stops.campa: Her film debut is shot in New York because her Broadway contract will not release her to Los Angeles. The picture needs Argentina; it gets a soundstage and borrowed exteriors, and a Brazilian singing in Portuguese with Brazilian musicians stands in for Buenos Aires. Argentine critics object that nothing in it is Argentine. In Buenos Aires that year Eva Duarte is a radio actress working the same manufactured-icon machinery from the other bank of the Plata. The film grosses about two million dollars, and Hollywood decides it has found a category.
suggested_refs: Down Argentine Way (1940), Twentieth Century-Fox, filmed partly in New York

stops.name: Copacabana Palace, the return to Rio
stops.date_confidence: the return date is attested; her lodging at this hotel is tradition, not documented
stops.campa: She comes home for the first time since 1939, to a cheering crowd at the docks, and takes rooms at the Copacabana Palace, the oceanfront hotel that has been Rio's stage for foreign glamour since the twenties. That she stayed there on this trip is biographical tradition and is confirmed by no document in the sourcing gathered. The welcome lasts about five days. Then the newspapers and the drawing rooms begin, and the word they use is americanizada.
suggested_refs: The Copacabana Palace Hotel, Rio de Janeiro, lodging unconfirmed for the 1940 visit

stops.name: Cassino da Urca, the return engagement
stops.date_confidence: contested; sources place the booing here and at the charity concert five days later, and the sourcing gathered does not resolve which
stops.campa: She plays a return engagement at the Urca, the room that sent her north, and greets the audience in English before opening with 'South American Way.' The elite that made her expects Brazil carried triumphantly abroad and hears an American act instead. Accounts differ on where exactly the booing happened, some placing it here and some at the charity concert five days later. What every account agrees on is that she was booed, in Rio, by the class that had been proudest of her.
suggested_refs: The 1940 return engagement at the Cassino da Urca, contested in the sources
sources: josmarlopes.wordpress.com, 'Two Brazilian Charmers: Carmen Goes Bananas'

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the Darcy Vargas charity concert
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: At a charity concert organized by the first lady, Darcy Vargas, the audience meets her with silence and then with booing. She finishes and weeps in her dressing room. The charge is double and self-contradicting: that she has sold Brazil to American commerce, and that the Brazil she sells is too black, the dress of Bahian street vendors carried into rooms where such women are servants. The Estado Novo that paid her band's passage north does not defend her. She leaves, and does not come back for fourteen years.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to an unnamed Brazilian newspaper, 1940; the phrase recurs in secondary accounts of the homecoming and no primary text could be traced [R]
suggested_refs: The Darcy Vargas charity concert, Rio de Janeiro, 15 July 1940
sources: Luz Media, 'The Polarizing Legacy of Carmen Miranda'

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the Odeon session
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: She answers in the only language the argument is being conducted in. 'Disseram que Voltei Americanizada' is recorded for Odeon on the second of September, written by Luiz Peixoto and Vicente Paiva: a samba about being accused of ceasing to be Brazilian, sung in Portuguese, in Rio, by the woman accused. Later she records 'Bananas Is My Business,' which does the same work in English about the same caricature. Then she sails, and the answer stands as the last thing she says to the country in person for fourteen years.
stops.quote: Disseram que eu voltei americanizada / Com o burro do dinheiro / Que eu estou muito rica
stops.quote_source: Opening lines of 'Disseram que Voltei Americanizada,' Luiz Peixoto and Vicente Paiva, recorded for Odeon 2 September 1940; text per cancioneros.com and Brazilian lyrics archives
suggested_refs: The Odeon recording of 'Disseram que Voltei Americanizada,' 2 September 1940

stops.name: Grauman's Chinese Theatre, the cement
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: She presses hands, feet, and a pair of platform heels into the forecourt cement at Grauman's Chinese Theatre, the first Latin American to do it. The concrete fixes her in the Hollywood landscape at the same moment the landscape is reducing her to a hat. The Walk of Fame star that many accounts attach to this date does not exist yet and cannot: the Walk is not created until 1958 and its first stars are laid in 1960. Hers comes then, posthumously, and in the television category.
suggested_refs: The forecourt imprints at Grauman's Chinese Theatre, 24 March 1941

stops.name: Twentieth Century-Fox, That Night in Rio
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted, and the soundstage coordinate is approximate on the Pico Boulevard lot
stops.campa: Fox builds Rio de Janeiro on a Los Angeles backlot and casts a woman from Rio inside the fabrication. She does not set foot in the city during production. The same year the studio builds Havana on the same lot for Week-End in Havana, which tops the box office and reportedly outgrosses Citizen Kane. Rio, Havana, Buenos Aires: the studio treats them as one country and her as its one available citizen. In 1942 Fox pays Lee Shubert sixty thousand dollars to end his claim on her and hold her whole.
stops.quote: [Don] Ameche is very capable in a dual role, and Miss [Alice] Faye is eye-appealing but it's the tempestuous Miranda who really gets away to a flying start from the first sequence.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to a Variety review of That Night in Rio, 1941, as quoted in English Wikipedia; the original Variety text could not be reached [R]
suggested_refs: That Night in Rio (1941) and Week-End in Havana (1941), Twentieth Century-Fox

stops.name: Twentieth Century-Fox, The Gang's All Here
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Busby Berkeley builds 'The Lady in the Tutti-Frutti Hat' on the Fox lot: a chorus of women with six-foot bananas, and Miranda at the center under a turban that grows past the top of the frame. The film ranks among the ten highest-grossing releases of the year. The number outlives the film, the studio, and her. It becomes the fixed public image of Carmen Miranda, with the samba tradition and the Brazilian radio career that actually made her stripped out of it.
stops.quote: That she should be best remembered for her hats undercuts her talent.
stops.quote_source: Greg S. Faller, entry on Carmen Miranda, International Dictionary of Films and Filmmakers, quoted on Encyclopedia.com
suggested_refs: The Lady in the Tutti-Frutti Hat, The Gang's All Here (1943), directed by Busby Berkeley
sources: English Wikipedia, 'The Lady in the Tutti Frutti Hat'

stops.name: Hollywood, the highest-paid woman in the United States
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the earnings figure is reported, not audited
stops.campa: She is reported the highest-paid woman in the United States, earning over two hundred thousand dollars a year, and she is designing and building most of what she wears while she does it. Two years earlier Madame Chiang Kai-shek had addressed Congress as a foreign woman America had already decided it knew, an image assembled for wartime American consumption on the same terms and in the same years. Miranda's terms include a turban and a language nobody in the audience speaks.
suggested_refs: Reported 1945 earnings of Carmen Miranda, cited without an underlying tax record

stops.name: Twentieth Century-Fox, the contract lapses
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the January date is a convention of the sourcing, not a documented event
stops.campa: The Fox contract expires and is not renewed. The postwar pictures are shot in black and white, which removes the one thing the studio ever wanted from her, and the wartime hemispheric-goodwill program that imported her has no further use for a Latin American face now that the war is won. She is thirty-seven, at the top of her earning, and the machinery that built the image has finished with it. The image does not stop. It detaches from her and goes on by itself.
suggested_refs: The lapse of the Twentieth Century-Fox contract, 1946

stops.name: Hollywood, Copacabana with Groucho Marx
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: She makes Copacabana independently, opposite Groucho Marx, playing a singer who invents a second identity behind a veil because one performer cannot get two bookings. She plays both. On the set she meets David Sebastian, a producer, and marries him within months. The film is named for the Rio beach she grew up near and shot nowhere near it. The supper-club economy the title borrows from is the same circuit Meyer Lansky and Lucky Luciano are running out of Havana in these same years.
suggested_refs: Copacabana (1947), United Artists, with Groucho Marx

stops.name: Church of the Good Shepherd, the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: She marries David Sebastian at the Church of the Good Shepherd in Beverly Hills. She is thirty-eight and has worked without a real break since she was fourteen. She becomes pregnant the following year and miscarries after performing a show. The marriage is bad early and stays bad, by her own later accounts running to violence and heavy drinking on both sides; she announces a separation in September 1949 and reconciles within months. It holds on paper until she dies. He is the one who finds her.
suggested_refs: The Church of the Good Shepherd, Beverly Hills, marriage of 17 March 1947

stops.name: Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, Culver City, A Date with Judy
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: MGM picks her up after Fox lets her go. In A Date with Judy the studio takes off the turban, restyles her hair and puts her in evening gowns, testing whether there is a performer under the costume that an audience will pay for. There is, and they do not. She makes Nancy Goes to Rio for the same studio in 1950, another Rio built in Culver City, twenty-three years after the milliner's shop and six thousand miles from the beach in the title. The MGM run is short. By now the caricature is public property and needs no film to sustain it.
suggested_refs: A Date with Judy (1948) and Nancy Goes to Rio (1950), MGM, Culver City

stops.name: Hollywood, the Decca sides with the Andrews Sisters
stops.date_confidence: the 1948-1950 recording period is attested; the recording city is not documented, so the corpus Hollywood pin is used
stops.campa: She cuts three records with the Andrews Sisters for Decca between 1948 and 1950. 'Cuanto Le Gusta' reaches number twelve on the Billboard chart and is the last American hit of her life. The Andrews Sisters are the house sound of American wartime cheer, and she is folded into it as the exotic top note, singing Spanish over a close-harmony trio from Minnesota. Where the sessions were cut is not stated in the sourcing gathered; the stop sits on the general coordinate for Hollywood.
suggested_refs: The Decca sides of Carmen Miranda with the Andrews Sisters, 1948-1950

stops.name: Copacabana nightclub, New York
stops.date_confidence: tradition; the engagements recur in secondary accounts with no documented date, so a late-1940s year is defaulted
stops.campa: She plays the Copacabana off Fifth Avenue, New York's supper club of record, named for the Rio beach with no comment from anyone. The booking measures how far the act has traveled from Brazilian radio: it lives in American nightclubs now, and Brazil is a costume she puts on rather than a place she goes. Her engagements at the club recur in secondary accounts without a documented date attached, so this stop rests on tradition and is placed in the late forties for want of anything firmer.
suggested_refs: The Copacabana nightclub, East Sixtieth Street, New York, engagement dates unverified
sources: General nightclub-circuit tradition in the Carmen Miranda literature (unverified)

stops.name: Hollywood, Scared Stiff, the last film
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Her last film is Scared Stiff, a Paramount comedy with Dean Martin and Jerry Lewis. She comes on, sings, and leaves the plot exactly where she found it. Martin and Lewis are what the picture is about; she is the number it stops for. She is forty-four, and it is thirteen years since Down Argentine Way. The image she assembled out of a Bahian street dress and a milliner's training has become a costume any comedian can put on, and she is on the set watching it worn back at her.
suggested_refs: Scared Stiff (1953), Paramount, her final film appearance

stops.name: Cincinnati, the collapse
stops.date_confidence: month attested; the day is not given in the sourcing and is defaulted
stops.campa: On tour she collapses from exhaustion while performing in Cincinnati. She has been working through smoking, drinking, amphetamines to get on and barbiturates to come down, on a schedule that has not paused since Broadway in 1939. She is forty-four, and the tour has run through Europe and back across the United States without a pause long enough to matter. The reports in the sourcing gathered give the month and not the day. This is the first public sign that the body doing the work is failing, and there are twenty-two months left.
suggested_refs: The October 1953 Cincinnati collapse during her US and European tour

stops.name: LeRoy Sanitarium, New York
stops.date_confidence: month attested; the coordinate is derived from the sanitarium's street address, not from a source that supplies one
stops.campa: She is admitted to the LeRoy Sanitarium at 40 East Sixty-first Street in Lenox Hill, a private hospital founded in 1928 and closed in 1980. Several accounts place the sanitarium in Cincinnati alongside the collapse; it is in New York, and she was moved. The diagnosis in the reachable sourcing is exhaustion, which in 1953 is the word used instead of the other words, and no medical record from the admission is quoted anywhere in that sourcing. She rests, and then she goes back to work, and the schedule closes over the gap.
suggested_refs: The LeRoy Sanitarium, 40 East 61st Street, New York, 1928-1980

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the return after fourteen years
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: She returns to Rio on the third of December, fourteen years after the booing, and stays four months. The city that turned on her in 1940 receives her back without settling anything; the argument about whether she sold Brazil or carried it is suspended while she is standing in it. She sails on the fourth of April 1955. Four months after that she is dead, and the argument resumes without her, and runs on for the rest of the century in the mouths of people who were children when she left.
stops.quote: For generations of musicians who were adolescents in the second half of the 1950s and became adults at the height of the Brazilian military dictatorship and the international wave of counterculture, my generation, Carmen Miranda was first a cause of both pride and shame.
stops.quote_source: Caetano Veloso, op-ed, The New York Times, 20 October 1991, quoted in Remezcla
suggested_refs: Her four-month Rio residence, 3 December 1954 to 4 April 1955

stops.name: New Frontier Hotel, Las Vegas
stops.date_confidence: month attested in the late-career touring chronology; the hotel is demolished and the coordinate is the historic Strip site
stops.campa: She works the New Frontier on the Strip a few months before she dies, still on the circuit, with a heart damaged by two decades of amphetamines and a schedule nobody would now be permitted to keep. Las Vegas is absorbing the supper-club stars whose studio contracts have run out, and she is one of them. The hotel is long demolished. It is among the last documented stage appearances of her life, and the sourcing for it is a touring chronology rather than a contract.
suggested_refs: The New Frontier Hotel, Las Vegas Strip, demolished
sources: General late-career touring chronology (unverified against a booking record)

stops.name: Hollywood, the Jimmy Durante taping
stops.date_confidence: attested; the NBC building is not independently confirmed and the coordinate is the corpus Hollywood pin
stops.campa: She films a musical segment for NBC's The Jimmy Durante Show. During the number 'Jackson, Miranda and Gomez' she drops to one knee; Durante reaches for her, she says she is out of breath, she gets up and finishes it, and afterward performs again informally for the cast and the technicians. The segment is not live and airs after her death. The same year, on the same Hollywood television circuit, Caterina Valente makes her American debut as a European curiosity who sings in whichever language the sponsor prefers.
suggested_refs: The Jimmy Durante Show segment filmed 4 August 1955, broadcast posthumously

stops.name: Beverly Hills, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested; the street address is not verified and the coordinate is a city fix, the same one used for the marriage
stops.campa: She is found in a hallway of her Beverly Hills house at about half past ten in the morning, dead of a heart attack at forty-six, hours after the taping and a party with the cast. She had gone to bed around three. Her husband finds her. She has worked continuously since she was fourteen and been famous continuously since she was twenty-one, and the segment filmed the previous afternoon has not yet been broadcast. The address is not verified in the reachable sourcing, so the coordinate marks the city and not the house.

stops.name: Palácio Pedro Ernesto, the lying in state
stops.date_confidence: attested; the sourcing names the town hall and the coordinate is the Palácio Pedro Ernesto on Cinelândia
stops.campa: Her body is flown to Rio at her own prior instruction and laid in state at the Palácio Pedro Ernesto, the city hall on Cinelândia, from the evening of the twelfth of August to the morning of the thirteenth. Roughly sixty thousand people file past. The coffin has been driven up from the docks at Praça Mauá, where the family came ashore in 1910. The government declares national mourning for a woman its own press had called americanizada fifteen years earlier.

stops.name: Central Rio de Janeiro, the cortège
stops.date_confidence: attested; the crowd figures vary by source and none is independently verifiable
stops.campa: An estimated half a million people line the route through central Rio for the funeral procession, one of the largest gatherings the city has seen, the casket under a Brazilian flag. Crowd figures vary widely across the sources gathered and none of them can be independently checked. The city that booed her at the Darcy Vargas concert stands in the street for her fifteen years later. Nothing between the two crowds is settled here; the second does not cancel the first.
stops.quote: No Brazilian woman has ever been as popular as Carmen Miranda, in Brazil or anywhere.
stops.quote_source: Ruy Castro, quoted in Mac Margolis, Newsweek International, 23 January 2006, reproduced on Encyclopedia.com

stops.name: Cemitério de São João Batista, the burial
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the day follows the cortège, and published coordinates for the cemetery vary by a few hundred meters
stops.campa: She is buried at the Cemitério de São João Batista in Botafogo, among Rio's political and cultural dead, in a tomb the family keeps plain. It becomes one of the most visited graves in the cemetery and stays that way. The Portuguese girl carried ashore at Praça Mauá in her mother's arms in 1910 ends as a daughter of Rio by the decision of half a million people in the street. Coordinates for the cemetery differ by a few hundred meters across the sources gathered.

stops.name: Hollywood Walk of Fame, the posthumous star
stops.date_confidence: the year and the address are attested; the date usually given, 8 February 1960, is the Walk's groundbreaking applied to the whole original batch rather than a dedication of her own
stops.campa: A star is laid for her on Hollywood Boulevard five years after her death, in the television category, at 6262 Hollywood Boulevard. The Walk of Fame did not exist while she was alive. She is the first South American honored on it, and she is honored for television by an industry that used her mainly to sell Technicolor. The star sits on a boulevard she worked for over a decade, six thousand miles from the cemetery in Botafogo where she was buried five years earlier.
stops.quote: Many of her compatriots never forgave her for the pastiche of mischief and malaprops that became not only Miranda's trademark Hollywood act but also synonymous with Latin America itself.
stops.quote_source: Mac Margolis, Newsweek International, 23 January 2006, quoted on Encyclopedia.com

stops.name: Museu Carmen Miranda, Flamengo Park
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Carmen Miranda Museum opens in Flamengo Park on the twenty-first anniversary of her death, in a circular pavilion designed by Affonso Eduardo Reidy and adapted by Ulisses Burlemaqui, decreed into existence twenty years before. It holds some three thousand five hundred and sixty objects, four hundred and sixty-one of them clothing: turbans, platform shoes, jewelry, eleven complete costumes. In 2009 a life-size resin figure is installed, cast from her death mask and her dental arch, wearing her own costume from That Night in Rio.
stops.quote: Carmen conquered 'white' America as no other South American has done or ever would.
stops.quote_source: Caetano Veloso, op-ed, The New York Times, 20 October 1991, quoted in Remezcla

stops.name: Carmen Miranda Square, Hollywood Boulevard
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: A stretch of Hollywood Boulevard at Orange Drive, across from the forecourt where she pressed her platform heels into the cement in 1941, is named Carmen Miranda Square, forty-three years after her death. In Rio in 1999 Augusto Boal stages a samba version of Bizet's Carmen, the opera her father loved and named her for, in the city where she is buried. Google marks her hundred and eighth birthday in 2017 with a drawing crediting the fruit hat to the baianas of Bahia rather than to Hollywood.
stops.quote: And later, a symbol that inspired the merciless gaze we began to cast upon ourselves.
